Musataha

Musataha lets a landowner put land to work without selling it.

The Structuring Brief · Issue 1 · 17 October 2026

On this page

  1. 01What Musataha is
  2. 02When it is used
  3. 03How it combines with Istisna’a and Ijara
  4. 04What to settle early
  5. 05How HAYKALAH has used it
  6. 06Related

Land that sits idle can cost money to hold and earn nothing. Selling it is one answer, but it gives up the land for good. Musataha is another: the owner keeps title and grants someone else the right to build on the land and use what they build, for an agreed term. This first issue of the Structuring Brief explains how Musataha works, when it is used, and how it combines with Istisna’a and Ijara to finance a building from the ground up.

01What Musataha is

Musataha is a right to build on and use land owned by another party for an agreed term, while the landowner keeps title to the land. It is also called a right to build, or a surface right.

The contract settles three things:

  • Who owns the land. The landowner grants the right and keeps title throughout the term.
  • Who builds and runs the asset. The holder of the right, usually a project company, builds the asset and runs it for the term.
  • What happens at the end. The contract sets what happens to the buildings when the term ends.

Because title stays with the landowner, a Musataha is not a sale. The owner gives up the use of the land for a period, not the land itself.

02When it is used

Musataha lets public and private landowners put land to work without selling it. Three situations where it is used:

  • A family or a company holds idle land. Musataha is one option alongside a joint venture, a lease (Ijara) or contributing the land in kind to a project company. Which one fits depends on the audit.
  • A public body owns land for a facility or a program. The land stays with the public owner while a project company builds and runs the asset.
  • An under-used asset goes through the asset-monetization engine. At the Structure step, Musataha sits alongside a concession, a JV SPV, an Ijara and a revenue share.

03How it combines with Istisna’a and Ijara

On its own, a Musataha settles the rights over the land. An Ijara or a Sukuk structure can sit on top of it, so that the rights over the land, the construction and the income are financed together. HAYKALAH’s Sukuk frameworks for public assets use this sequence:

  1. 1Musataha: the rights. The project company takes the right to build on and use the land for the term.
  2. 2Istisna’a: the construction. An Istisna’a is a contract to build a specified asset for an agreed price, which can be paid in stages while the asset is built. A financier can agree an Istisna’a with the client and a separate, parallel Istisna’a with the contractor who builds the asset.
  3. 3Ijara: the income. Once the asset is complete, it is leased under an Ijara. The lessee pays rent for its use, and where the structure is financed through Sukuk, the rent funds the distributions to the Sukuk holders.

The sequence puts the land, the construction phase and the income phase in one structure.

04What to settle early

These questions shape a Musataha and should be answered before the contract is drafted:

  • The term. How long the right lasts, and whether that is long enough for the asset’s income to repay what it cost to build.
  • The end of the term. What happens to the buildings when the term ends.
  • The use. What the holder may build, and how the asset may be used and leased.
  • The approvals. Shariah structures are subject to Shariah board approval, and offering Sukuk to investors is a regulated activity, executed through appropriately licensed partners.

05How HAYKALAH has used it

HAYKALAH uses Musataha in real-estate structuring, in its Sukuk frameworks for public assets, and in the asset-monetization engine as one way to put idle land to work.

On this website, the example that combines all three contracts is a proposal. In 2026 HAYKALAH proposed a Sukuk framework for stadium precincts: the issuer takes Musataha rights over the land, funds construction through Istisna’a, then moves the completed stadium to an Ijara or a Wakala-Ijara, with the rent paying the Sukuk holders. There is one issuer per stadium, across seven precincts for 2034. The framework is a proposal with no mandate, and its figures are withheld until the source documents are reconciled.

See the stadium explainer (Proposal)

Proposals are not mandates. Shariah structures are subject to Shariah board approval. Clients are not named until they consent.
